Amorous

AM-er-us -- from Latin amor ('love'); a distant cousin of this course's own word amity, from the same root. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Amorous is showing or feeling strong romantic love or desire.

Historians poring over the diplomat's private diary were startled by its unexpectedly amorous entries about a fellow attache.

Worked Example

The film's amorous subplot -- two rival scientists slowly falling for each other -- nearly outshone its actual plot about the moon landing.

The romantic feelings developing between the two scientists, separate from the main plot, are exactly what amorous describes.

How Amorous Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

romantic

romantic: relating to or characterized by feelings of love

enamored

enamored: filled with a feeling of love; captivated

Antonyms

indifferent

indifferent: having no particular interest or feeling

platonic

platonic: relating to a close relationship without romantic or sexual feeling

How Strong Is It? — romantic → amorous → enamored

romantic vs. amorous

romantic vs. amorous: Their romantic dinner ended with a walk along the pier at sunset.

enamored vs. amorous

enamored vs. amorous: Within a week of meeting her, he was hopelessly enamored, texting her name into every conversation.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — amor-

root — amor-: love (Latin (amor))

suffix — -ous

suffix — -ous: full of, having the quality of (Latin (-osus))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin amor ('love') plus -ous ('full of') -- amorous literally means 'full of love.' The same root appears in this course's own word amity, which names a friendly rather than romantic bond.

Use the root in a new word: enamored

Use the root in a new word: enamored: Enamored, meaning captivated by love, comes directly from that same Latin root, amor -- as does this course's own word amity, meaning a friendly relationship.

Root Check

Word Choice

Amorous specifically points to romantic or flirtatious feeling -- glances, letters, or a mood -- and is noticeably more old-fashioned and literary than everyday words like 'romantic.'
